name: Nasal breathing meta
lead: The nasal breathing meta is the looksmaxxing belief that habitually breathing through the nose, rather than the mouth, supports healthy facial development, jaw and midface structure, and appearance. It is closely associated with mewing, mouth taping and discussions of nasal surgery.

Medical literature does describe a relationship between chronic mouth breathing in children and facial growth patterns, sometimes called long face syndrome, though causation can run in either direction [1][2]. A systematic review and meta-analysis examined the effects of mouth breathing on facial skeletal development in children [3]. Evidence on adults is much thinner, and no study that the wiki has located tests whether adopting nasal breathing in adulthood changes facial appearance.

paras: Nasal breathing filters, warms and humidifies air, and nasal breathing is described as producing nitric oxide [1]. Chronic mouth breathing is reported to arise in most cases as an adaptation to nasal congestion, particularly during sleep [1]. Linked conditions include sleep apnea, snoring and anterior open bite [1].

Concern about mouth breathing is old: the painter and writer George Catlin published a book in 1862, later retitled Shut Your Mouth and Save Your Life, urging nose breathing, and a 1903 school hygiene book described a child with the typical face of a mouth-breather [1].

A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis assessed how mouth breathing affects facial skeletal development and malocclusion in children, pooling cephalometric measures such as jaw position, facial height and overjet [3]. A 2010 study compared mouth breathing and nasal breathing in orthodontic patients' dentofacial and craniofacial development [4]. A general reference notes that much of the evidence comes from textbooks, reviews and small studies, and that the health effects of mouth taping have been little researched [1]. The relationship may also run in reverse, with a long narrow face and narrow nasopharynx predisposing to nasal obstruction [1].

Functional rhinoplasty and septal or turbinate surgery are described in reviews as treatments for nasal obstruction [5]. Palatal expansion is discussed in some communities as a way to enlarge the nasal airway; clinical trials have measured nasal airflow after expansion in late adolescents and young adults [6]. External nasal strips such as Breathe Right have been studied for snoring in a polysomnographic trial [7].

On looksmax.org, users compare options such as maxillary expansion and turbinate reduction for nasal breathing problems. In one thread a user warns against turbinate reduction citing empty nose syndrome, while another replies that reduction is the treatment for blockage from enlarged turbinates and calls expansion procedures gimmicks [8]. Another encyclopedia article describes nasal breathing as a recommended habit among mewing proponents, who claim it supports airway development, and describes mouth taping as risky without professional supervision [9].

timeline.event: George Catlin publishes The Breath of Life, later retitled Shut Your Mouth and Save Your Life [1].
A school hygiene text describes a child with the typical face of a mouth-breather [1].
Systematic review and meta-analysis of mouth breathing and facial skeletal development in children [3].

lore.intro: Nasal breathing is treated in these communities as a foundation habit for facial development and airway, linked to mewing and sometimes to surgical options [8][9].

claims.claim: Mouth breathing narrows the face and recedes the jaw
claims.believers: Proponents say chronic mouth breathing alters growth toward a long, narrow face, and that nasal breathing supports airway and jaw development [9].
claims.experts: A 2021 meta-analysis examined mouth breathing and facial skeletal development in children, and a general reference says the relationship may run in both directions with limited high-quality evidence [1][3].

claims.claim: Switching to nasal breathing as an adult improves facial appearance
claims.believers: Mewing-related discussions recommend nasal breathing as part of improving the face and reducing snoring [9].
claims.experts: No published study has tested adult appearance changes from nasal breathing; the child studies concern growth [3].

claims.claim: Mouth taping helps maintain nasal breathing during sleep
claims.believers: Mouth taping is practiced to keep the lips closed at night [1].
claims.experts: A reference article states that benefits of mouth taping are little researched, and another says it is risky without professional supervision [1][9].

claims.claim: Surgery or expansion can fix nasal breathing problems
claims.believers: Forum users debate turbinate reduction versus maxillary expansion, with divergent views on risk [8].
claims.experts: Reviews describe functional rhinoplasty and related surgery for obstruction, and trials have measured nasal airflow after palatal expansion [5][6].

card.summary: Breathing through the nose for better facial development; child studies link mouth breathing to growth changes, adult appearance effects are untested.
card.note: Mouth taping is little studied and described as risky without supervision.

quick.overview:
The nasal breathing meta says habitual nose breathing supports facial development and airway, and mouth breathing leads to a long narrow face.

Research connects chronic mouth breathing to growth patterns in children, but the link may run both ways and no study tests adult appearance changes.
quick.mechanism: Proponents say breathing pattern and tongue posture influence the growing jaw and midface. In medicine, nasal obstruction causes mouth breathing, and treatment focuses on the obstruction.
quick.risks: Breathing through the nose is normal physiology. Mouth taping is little researched, and nasal surgery such as turbinate reduction carries surgical risks, with empty nose syndrome raised by some users.
